t: Split Array With Same Average — Meet in the Middle & Bitset DP
o: We must partition `nums` into two non-empty groups whose averages are equal. If group A has size $k$ and sum $s$, then $s/k = S/n$ where $S$ is the total sum, so we only need to find **any** non-empty proper subset whose sum equals $k \cdot S / n$. This transforms an average-matching problem into a subset-sum existence problem. In example 1 ($n=8$, $S=36$, average 4.5) we need a subset of size $k$ with sum $4.5k$: e.g. $k=4$, sum 18 — `[1,4,5,8]` works. In example 2 ($S=4$, $n=2$), sizes 1 require sum 2, but elements are 3 and 1, so no valid split exists. With $n \le 30$ there are up to $2^{30}$ subsets — too many to enumerate directly, but small enough for meet-in-the-middle or a pseudo-polynomial DP on (size, sum).
k: Equal averages reduce to: does a subset of size $k$ exist with sum exactly $k \cdot S / n$ for some $1 \le k \le n-1$?
Only one side of the split needs to be found; checking $k \le n/2$ suffices since the complement covers larger sizes.
Meet in the middle turns $2^{30}$ into about $2 \cdot 2^{15}$ enumerated subsets joined by hash lookups.
A bitset DP indexed by (subset size, achievable sum) runs in roughly $O(n^2 \cdot S / 64)$ time.

a.i: Split the array into two halves and enumerate all subsets of each half, recording sums grouped by subset size. A full solution uses $a$ elements from the left half (sum $s_a$) and $b$ from the right (sum $s_b$); the condition $(s_a+s_b)/ (a+b) = S/n$ rearranges to $n(s_a+s_b) = (a+b)S$, so for each left subset we can compute the exact right-side sum needed and hash-lookup it among right subsets of matching size. Enumerating each half costs at most $2^{15}$ subsets.
s: Compute total sum S; quick answer true if all elements are equal (any single-element vs rest split works).
Enumerate every subset of the left half, storing map[size] -> set of sums; same for the right half.
For each left subset of size a and sum sa, for each right size b (with 1 <= a+b <= n-1), solve n*(sa+sb) == (a+b)*S for sb; skip if not a non-negative integer.
Return true if the required sb exists in the right-half map for size b.
If no combination matches, return false.
a.t: O(2^(n/2) * n) time — enumerating ~2^15 subsets per half plus pairwise size/sum checks.
a.sp: O(2^(n/2)) space for the stored subset sums per half.

a.n: Approach 2: Bitset Dynamic Programming over (size, sum)
a.i: For each possible subset size $k$ from 1 to $n/2$, ask whether some $k$ elements sum to exactly $kS/n$ (only when $kS$ is divisible by $n$). Maintain `dp[k]` as a bitmask (big integer / bitset) where bit $s$ means "some $k$ elements sum to $s$". Processing each number and updating sizes in decreasing order gives standard 0/1-knapsack semantics. Since sums are bounded by $30 \times 10^4 = 300{,}000$, big-integer shifts make this very fast in practice.
s: Compute total S; if no k in 1..n/2 satisfies k*S % n == 0, return false immediately.
Initialize dp[0] = 1 (bit 0 set), representing the empty subset.
For each num, iterate k from high to low: dp[k+1] |= dp[k] << num.
After processing, for each k with k*S % n == 0, check whether bit (k*S/n) is set in dp[k]; also ensure the complement is non-empty (k < n).
Return true if any such k passes, else false.
a.t: O(n^2 * S / w) time with word-size w (bitset speedup); the JS Set variant is O(n^2 * distinct sums).
a.sp: O(n * S) bits for the DP table (~9 MB as C++ bitsets, fine within limits).

w: In an interview, start from the key reduction (subset of size k with sum kS/n), then present the bitset DP as the primary solution — it is simpler to reason about and fast enough given S ≤ 300,000. Mention meet-in-the-middle as the alternative when values were unbounded but n ≤ 30. Pitfalls: forgetting that only k ≤ n/2 needs checking (the complement covers the rest), integer division when testing divisibility of k*S by n, zero elements (averages of 0 work fine — e.g. `[0,0]` returns true), and overflow of k*S in fixed-width languages (use 64-bit). Edge cases: n = 1 always false (can't form two non-empty parts); all-equal arrays always true. Follow-ups may ask to output the actual split (track parent pointers or reconstruct from the two halves) or handle negative numbers (offset sums by a constant).
